rows.claim: residual copper above roughly 0.5 mg/L
rows.note: Residual copper as a pro-oxidant catalyst above ~0.5 mg/L is plausible and broadly consistent with the fact that both the OIV limit (1 mg/L) and the older/current US TTB residual limit (historically 0.5 mg/L, per the TTB Federal Register material found) sit in this range, but no source directly states 0.5 mg/L as a pro-oxidant threshold specifically.

rows.claim: A must fermenting to 12-13% abv needs of the order of 150 mg N/L
rows.note: ~150 mg N/L YAN requirement for a must fermenting to 12-13% abv is a commonly cited rule of thumb (Zoecklein-school figures), not independently sourced to a tier-1 document in this pass.

rows.claim: roughly 25-30 mg N/L for every 1% of potential alcohol
rows.note: 25-30 mg N/L per 1% potential alcohol scaling rule not independently sourced this pass.

rows.claim: a shelf price under about 7 in the UK
rows.note: 7 pound UK retail threshold is a framing device tied to current duty/VAT/market levels, which move over time.

rows.claim: leaves of the order of 50p a litre for the wine
rows.note: ~50p/litre residual wine-cost estimate is illustrative commercial arithmetic, not independently sourced, and duty-sensitive.

rows.claim: a molecular SO2 target of 0.8 mg/L, which at pH 3.2 needs roughly 25-30 mg/L free

source.ref: Avoiding spoilage caused by lactic acid bacteria
source.quote: Lactic acid bacteria are more sensitive to SO2 than yeast and a molecular SO2 concentration of 0.8 mg/L will inhibit their growth.

rows.claim: is capped at 200 mg/L and used at 150-200 mg/L

source.ref: CHEMICAL OPTIONS FOR MICROBIOLOGICAL STABILISATION - Sorbic acid

rows.claim: sugar above 4 g/L and up to 12 g/L

source.ref: International Code of Oenological Practices - Complementary definitions relating to sugar content (oiv.int)
source.quote: Medium dry, when the sugar content of the wine is higher than [4 g/l, or 9 g/l under the acidity exception] and does not exceed 12 g/l or 18 g/l, when the difference between the sugar content and the level of total acidity... does not exceed 10 g/l.

rows.note: This is the exact OIV/EU (Reg 2019/33 Annex III) sweetness-category definition, corroborated independently by the Czech and Austrian national wine-labelling guidance pages found in the same search.

rows.claim: up to 18 g/L where total acidity is within 10 g/L of the sugar figure

source.ref: International Code of Oenological Practices - Complementary definitions relating to sugar content (oiv.int)
source.quote: ...18 g/l, when the difference between the sugar content and the level of total acidity expressed in g/l of tartaric acid does not exceed 10g/l.

rows.claim: detectable from around 5-6 g/L in a high-acid wine
rows.note: 5-6 g/L sweetness detection threshold in a high-acid wine is a plausible sensory figure but not independently sourced this pass.

rows.claim: Fruit picked at 11-12% potential alcohol gives a finished wine of 10.5-11.5% abv
rows.note: Basic fermentation-yield arithmetic (11-12% potential alcohol giving 10.5-11.5% finished after RS is retained) is low-risk illustrative reasoning, not a specific external fact to source.

rows.claim: Ferment cool, at 13-16
rows.note: 13-16C cool ferment range for off-dry whites is standard practice, not independently sourced this pass.

rows.claim: chilling the tank to 2-4
rows.note: Chilling to 2-4C to arrest fermentation is standard practice, not independently sourced this pass.

rows.claim: sterile membrane filtration at 0.45 microns

source.ref: Avoiding spoilage caused by lactic acid bacteria
source.quote: sterile filtration through 0.45 micron membranes may be required to completely remove the bacteria and achieve microbial stability.

rows.claim: Dimethyl dicarbonate, capped at 200 mg/L in the EU

source.publisher: IVES Technical Reviews (usage example) / general EU DMDC regulatory cap
source.ref: Lowering wine alcohol content by reverse osmosis and spinning cone columns (IVES)
source.quote: Before bottling, to avoid microbiological deterioration of the beverages, 180 mg/hL and 200 mg/L of sorbate and dimethyl dicarbonate was added respectively.

rows.note: 200 mg/L is both the dose actually used in a published IVES study and the widely-cited EU/US regulatory ceiling for DMDC (Velcorin); the IVES usage matches the claimed cap.

rows.claim: a new 225-litre barrel admits of the order of 20-30 mg/L of oxygen a year
rows.note: Duplicate of th_2016_p2_q2#2 - 20-30 mg/L/year barrel oxygen ingress figure not located in a tier-1 source this pass despite appearing twice in the corpus; worth a dedicated source hunt (Vivas & Glories / Ribereau-Gayon Handbook of Enology Vol 2) before the exam.

rows.claim: Below about pH 3.4 a given free SO2 delivers far more molecular SO2

source.ref: Molecular SO2/pH relationship, corroborated across sources
source.quote: A good estimate of the level of molecular sulfur dioxide in wine can be made using the free sulfur dioxide and pH values (ETS); Most winemakers are fully aware of the relationship between pH and molecular free sulfur dioxide (VT).

rows.claim: at pH 3.2 some 25 mg/L free SO2 gives the 0.8 mg/L molecular target, where at pH 3.8 it takes nearer 75 mg/L

source.publisher: Computed from SO2/pH equilibrium chemistry, anchored to AWRI's 0.8 mg/L target
source.ref: AWRI-confirmed molecular SO2 target (0.8 mg/L) combined with the standard sulfurous-acid pKa1 (~1.8) used in the Henderson-Hasselbalch molecular-SO2 calculation
source.quote: Fraction molecular = 1/(1+10^(pH-pKa1)); at pH3.2 with pKa1=1.81, fraction approx 3.9%, so free SO2 needed for 0.8 mg/L molecular approx 20.5 mg/L; at pH3.8, fraction approx 1.0%, so free SO2 needed approx 79 mg/L.

rows.corrected_claim: Using the standard SO2 equilibrium calculation, achieving 0.8 mg/L molecular SO2 requires roughly 20 mg/L free SO2 at pH 3.2 (the claim's '25 mg/L' runs a little high) and roughly 79 mg/L at pH 3.8 (closely matching the claim's 'nearer 75 mg/L').
rows.note: Independently recomputed from first principles (Henderson-Hasselbalch with standard pKa1); the pH3.8 figure matches closely, the pH3.2 figure is a bit optimistic (calculated ~20mg/L vs claimed ~25mg/L) - small enough to be within normal table-rounding/pKa-convention variance, but worth a source check against a published AWRI/Iland molecular-SO2 table.

rows.claim: Total package oxygen at bottling, which for a wine intended to age should be held under about 1 mg/L

source.ref: Fact Sheet TPO_Final - Understanding total package oxygen
source.quote: Most modern bottling lines are able to achieve displacement of approximately 60-80% of the oxygen from the headspace, resulting in reasonably low HO values of around 0.8-1.5 mg/L. / DO is minimised... to reduce or keep the DO below 0.5 mg/L.

rows.corrected_claim: AWRI's own figures suggest that even a well-run bottling line typically delivers DO under 0.5 mg/L plus HO of ~0.8-1.5 mg/L, meaning total package oxygen for premium age-worthy wines commonly runs to roughly 1.5-2 mg/L rather than reliably under 1 mg/L; 'under about 1 mg/L' is an aspirational best-in-class target rather than a typical achieved figure.
rows.note: Directionally correct (minimise TPO for ageing wines) but the specific 'under about 1 mg/L' figure is optimistic against AWRI's own component figures (DO + HO alone can sum above 1 mg/L on a good line, before closure-encapsulated oxygen is added).

rows.claim: a tin-lined screwcap admits very little, an engineered technical cork a specified amount, and a synthetic closure a great deal more

source.ref: 248 Technical Review October 2020 - Summary of AWRI closure trials
source.quote: Screwcaps have the lowest OTR but still vary depending on the lining used... the best performing natural corks have OTRs comparable to screwcaps.

rows.note: AWRI closure-trial data confirm screwcaps at the low end and a wide range of OTR among natural/technical/synthetic closures; the general ranking (screwcap lowest, synthetic generally highest) is standard, well-supported closure science, though AWRI notes some natural corks can match the best screwcaps.

rows.claim: Dissolved CO2 is the cheapest lever of all: 500-700 mg/L reads as freshness in a young white, under 400 mg/L reads as flat
rows.note: Dissolved CO2 freshness thresholds (500-700 mg/L fresh vs <400 mg/L flat) are commonly cited winemaking figures, not independently sourced this pass.

rows.claim: Oenological tannins are added at 5-20 g/hL
rows.note: Oenological tannin addition rate 5-20 g/hL is a plausible standard dosing range; an IVES paper found in this pass used a much higher 2 g/L (200 g/hL) dose, but that was for a specific dealcoholised-wine correction case, not standard grip-restoring dosing, so it does not contradict the claim.

rows.claim: gum arabic at 100-250 mg/L
rows.note: Gum arabic 100-250 mg/L is a standard cited dosing range, not independently sourced this pass.

rows.claim: roughly 5-6 bar in a traditional-method sparkling wine against 1-2.5 bar in a frizzante
rows.note: Sparkling wine pressure classifications (traditional method ~5-6 bar vs frizzante 1-2.5 bar) are well-known EU regulatory categories (spumante/frizzante distinction), but a tier-1 source stating these exact bar figures was not located in this specific pass.

rows.claim: brut nature at under 3 g/L reads leaner and more angular than a demi-sec
rows.note: Brut Nature's <3 g/L legal definition is a standard EU sparkling-wine dosage category; a tier-1 source confirming the exact 3 g/L threshold was not located in this specific pass (though it is consistent with widely published sparkling dosage tables).

rows.claim: fortifying to about 19-20% abv while some 90-100 g/L of sugar remains
rows.note: Vintage Port fortification to ~19-20% abv with ~90-100 g/L residual sugar is a commonly cited range in Port literature; a tier-1 IVDP source confirming these exact figures was not located in this specific pass.

rows.claim: molecular SO2 of 0.5-0.6 mg/L for a dry red and 0.8 mg/L where sugar is present

source.ref: Spoilage issues in Pinot Noir (https://www.awri.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/s2105.pdf) and Avoiding spoilage caused by lactic acid bacteria (https://www.awri.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2011/06/Avoiding-spoilage-from-LAB.pdf)
source.quote: The AWRI generally recommends that a concentration of 0.6mg/L of molecular SO2 be achieved in red wines to inhibit the growth of bacteria and yeast ... Lactic acid bacteria are more sensitive to SO2 than yeast and a molecular SO2 concentration of 0.8 mg/L will inhibit their growth.

rows.corrected_claim: a molecular SO2 target of about 0.6 mg/L for a dry red, rising to 0.8 mg/L where microbial risk is higher, including wines holding residual sugar
rows.note: The two figures are real and tier-1 sourced, but the answer attaches 0.8 mg/L to 'where sugar is present'. AWRI attaches 0.8 mg/L to inhibition of lactic acid bacteria generally, and gives 0.6 (not 0.5-0.6) as the red-wine recommendation. An examiner who knows the AWRI position would mark the attribution, not the number.

rows.claim: at pH 3.4 that is roughly 30 mg/L free, at pH 3.8 nearer 75 mg/L

source.ref: Avoiding spoilage caused by lactic acid bacteria (https://www.awri.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2011/06/Avoiding-spoilage-from-LAB.pdf)
source.quote: the pH and SO2 concentration should be such that >0.6 mg/L of molecular SO2 is present in the wine just after bottling. For example, if the pH is 3.5, then the free SO2 concentration should be at least 30 mg/L.

rows.corrected_claim: at pH 3.4 that is roughly 25 mg/L free, at pH 3.5 about 30 mg/L, and at pH 3.8 nearer 60 mg/L
rows.note: The AWRI's own anchor point is pH 3.5 = 30 mg/L free for 0.6 mg/L molecular. On the same dissociation relationship (pKa 1.81) 0.6 molecular needs ~24 mg/L at pH 3.4 and ~59 mg/L at pH 3.8. The answer's figures (30 and 75) correspond to about 0.75 mg/L molecular, so they are internally inconsistent with the 0.5-0.6 target stated in the same sentence, and ~25% high. This is exactly the sort of pair a candidate memorises together and gets caught on.

rows.claim: held below about 1 mg/L for an age-worthy white

source.ref: Pre-bottling wine adjustments and specifications (https://www.awri.com.au/industry_support/winemaking_resources/storage-and-packaging/pre-packaging-preparation/pre-bottling-wine-adjustments-and-specifications/) and Revisiting sulfur dioxide use (https://www.awri.com.au/industry_support/winemaking_resources/fining-stabilities/microbiological/avoidance/sulfur_dioxide)
source.quote: | **Dissolved oxygen** | mg/L | <1.0 | ... the concentration of DO in wine increases by about 0.5 mg/L during bottling under ideal, industry best practice conditions, and will commonly be in the range of 1.0 to 1.5 mg/L when conditions are less than ideal.

rows.corrected_claim: dissolved oxygen held below about 1 mg/L for an age-worthy white, with total package oxygen — dissolved plus headspace — specified separately and higher
rows.note: AWRI's <1.0 mg/L target is for dissolved oxygen. Total package oxygen is DO plus headspace oxygen and is by definition the larger number, so applying a single 1 mg/L ceiling to both conflates two different measurements. The sentence is right in spirit and wrong in the detail an examiner in this subject would notice.

rows.claim: the EU volatile acidity ceiling, of the order of 1.2 g/L expressed as acetic acid

source.publisher: EUR-Lex (Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/934, Annex I Part C)
source.quote: The volatile acid content may not exceed: (a) 18 milliequivalents per litre for partially fermented grape must; (b) 18 milliequivalents per litre for white and rosé wines; or (c) 20 milliequivalents per litre for red wines.

rows.note: 20 meq/L x 60.05 mg/mmol = 1.20 g/L acetic acid, so 1.2 g/L is exactly the red-wine ceiling. Whites and rosés are tighter at 18 meq/L (1.08 g/L), and derogations exist for certain PDO and overripe-grape wines. The answer's hedge 'of the order of' carries it.

rows.claim: alcohol must be within the 0.5% abv label tolerance

source.publisher: DEFRA / UK legislation explanatory memorandum, citing Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/33 Article 44
source.quote: All labelling of wine will continue to be subject to the application of the 0.5% or 0.8% analytical tolerance provided for in Article 44 (Actual Alcoholic Strength) of Regulation (EU) No 2019/33.

rows.note: 0.5% vol is the standard tolerance and correct for a young still wine at bottling, which is the context. A wider 0.8% vol tolerance applies to certain categories (sparkling, liqueur, overripe-grape wines and wines stored in bottle for more than three years). I could not open Article 44's own text — the figure is confirmed via UK government and EUR-Lex documents quoting it, hence medium rather than high confidence.

rows.claim: ochratoxin A against the EU limit of 2 micrograms per kilogram

source.publisher: EUR-Lex (Commission Regulation (EC) No 1881/2006, Annex, point 2.2; now recast as Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915)
source.quote: maximum level of 2 µg/kg for wine (including sparkling wine) and grape juice

rows.note: Correct, including the fact that the limit is expressed per kilogram rather than per litre. Reg 1881/2006 was repealed and replaced by Reg (EU) 2023/915 in 2023, which carries the maximum levels forward — cite the current instrument if the answer names a regulation.

rows.claim: EU total SO2 ceilings of 150 mg/L for dry red and 200 mg/L for dry white

source.publisher: OIV (reproducing Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/934) and EUR-Lex
source.quote: EU White/Rosé < 5g/L sugars 200 ... Red < 5g/L sugars 150 ... Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/934

rows.note: Also confirmed: those ceilings apply below 5 g/L sugar; at or above 5 g/L they rise to 200 (red) and 250 (white/rosé). Flagged time_sensitive because the 2019/934 recital explicitly says the limits 'could be re-examined at a later date with a view to further reducing them'.

rows.claim: rising to 400 mg/L for the sweetest categories

source.publisher: EUR-Lex (Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/934, Annex I Part B, A.2(e))
source.quote: 400 milligrams per litre for: — wines entitled to the descriptions 'Beerenauslese', 'Ausbruch', 'Ausbruchwein', 'Trockenbeerenauslese', 'Strohwein', 'Schilfwein' and 'Eiswein' ... — white wines entitled to one of the following protected designations of origin: Sauternes, Barsac, Cadillac, Cérons, Loupiac, Sainte-Croix-du-Mont, Monbazillac, Bonnezeaux, Quarts de Chaume, Coteaux du Layon...

rows.note: The 400 mg/L tier is a named-category derogation (BA/TBA/Eiswein/Ausbruch/Strohwein plus a closed list of sweet white PDOs), not a general 'sweetest categories' allowance; a 300 mg/L tier sits below it. The answer's wording is loose but not wrong.

rows.claim: below 0.1-0.3 g/L confirms it is finished

source.quote: It is our experience that any measurable level of these nutrients can have the potential to act as a substrate for microbial growth. Winemakers should therefore be aiming to achieve concentrations below the detection limits for these nutrients, by enzymatic assay. These levels are 0.1 g/L for Glucose + Fructose, and 0.05 g/L for malic acid.

rows.corrected_claim: below about 0.1 g/L confirms it is finished — the AWRI target is under the enzymatic detection limit of 0.05 g/L
rows.note: The upper bound of the stated range is the problem. AWRI's position is that any measurable malic is a substrate, with 0.05 g/L the enzymatic detection limit; Cornell and OSU protocols both use <0.1 g/L (<50 mg/L) as 'MLF complete'. No tier-1 source treats 0.3 g/L residual malic as safe, and a candidate writing 0.3 g/L would be stating the opposite of best practice.

rows.claim: 0.45 micron membrane, which retains yeast and most spoilage bacteria, or 0.65 micron

source.quote: Surface filters are generally absolute filters with precisely defined maximum pore sizes and these include 0.65 µm and 0.45 µm or 'sterile' filtration. ... It is a long-held belief in the wine industry that tight surface filtration such as membrane or sterile filtration below 0.45 μm will strip the aroma and colour from 'big' red wines.

rows.note: AWRI notes the stripping concern is a 'long-held belief' and that modern non-polar membrane materials cause minimal colour adsorption, so the phenolic-stripping rationale for choosing 0.65 µm is industry practice rather than demonstrated fact.

rows.claim: Protein instability is assessed by a heat test at 80

source.quote: Heat the sample at 80°C for two hours. While six hours has been typical industry practice for the heat test, recent research has shown that two hours of heating time is sufficient.

rows.corrected_claim: Protein instability is assessed by a heat test at 80°C — two hours on current AWRI method, six on the older industry practice
rows.note: Temperature is right, duration is the superseded protocol. AWRI now specifies 2 hours heating and 3 hours cooling for white, rosé and red, and explicitly labels six hours as what 'has been typical industry practice'. A candidate quoting six hours is quoting the old method.

rows.claim: a turbidity rise above about 2 NTU calling for a bentonite trial

source.quote: | White wine | 2 hours | 3 hours | < 2.0 NTU | ... *Some laboratories require turbidity differences of <0.5 NTU for a pass result.

rows.note: AWRI's pass criterion is a turbidity difference <2.0 NTU across all three matrices, so a rise above 2 NTU is a fail and triggers bentonite. Worth knowing that some labs tighten this to <0.5 NTU.

rows.claim: Turbidity itself should be under 1 NTU for a bright white

source.ref: Pre-bottling wine adjustments and specifications (https://www.awri.com.au/industry_support/winemaking_resources/storage-and-packaging/pre-packaging-preparation/pre-bottling-wine-adjustments-and-specifications/) and Filtration – physical removal of microorganisms
source.quote: | **Turbidity** | NTU | <1.0 | <1.0 | <1.0 | <1.0 | – | ... A commonly used threshold for bottling is <1.0 NTU however an NTU reading of <1.0 is not necessarily a guarantee that the filter medium will not block up

rows.note: AWRI's pre-bottling target table gives <1.0 NTU for white, red and cask wines alike, so the figure is not specific to whites — but it is not wrong as written.

rows.claim: Copper above about 0.5 mg/L is a pro-oxidant and a casse risk, and the EU limit is 1 mg/L

source.publisher: AWRI; Virginia Tech Enology; EUR-Lex Reg (EU) 2019/934
source.quote: AWRI pre-bottling target: '| **Copper** | mg/L | <0.50 |' ; Virginia Tech: 'yeast fining is a practical means of removing excess copper (greater than 0.5 mg/L)' ; Reg 2019/934 (copper sulphate / copper citrate treatment): 'the copper content of the product so treated does not exceed 1 mg/l'

rows.note: Both halves check out. One nuance: the EU 1 mg/l is written as a condition attached to copper sulphate/copper citrate treatment (with 2 mg/l allowed for certain liqueur wines), rather than as a free-standing product limit — accurate enough for exam purposes.

rows.claim: Capacity is typically around 24,000 litres, and they are built either as a single vessel or divided into three or four sectional compartments
rows.note: Searched the KB (no bulk-transport or intermodal-container content at all) and tier-1 web (wineaustralia.com, oiv.int, nzwine.com, wosa.co.za, ec.europa.eu). The only sources carrying ISO tank capacities and compartment counts for wine are freight forwarders and flexitank manufacturers (Hillebrand Gori, SIA Flexitanks, Savino Del Bene, Bertling), which are commercial suppliers, not tier-1. Note also that 24,000 L is the figure those sources attach most often to flexitanks; for ISO tanks they give ranges without a single typical value. Recommend hedging to 'of the order of 24,000 litres'.

rows.claim: usually 16,000 to 26,000 litres
rows.note: Same search as q2#0. Commercial sources cluster on 'typically 16,000 to 24,000 litres', with 24,000 L the most-cited maximum (Hillebrand Gori's LCA is built on a 24,000-litre flexitank); I found nothing supporting a 26,000 L upper bound, tier-1 or otherwise. The lower bound and the general order of magnitude are consistent across sources. Suggest 'usually 16,000 to 24,000 litres'.

rows.claim: A 20ft container of packaged wine carries of the order of 9,000-10,000 bottles, some 7,000 litres
rows.note: Only source found is a flexitank manufacturer's CEO quoted in FreightWaves: 'You'll get 9,000 bottles of wine into a 20-foot container.' That is a supplier with an interest in the comparison, not tier-1, and 9,000 x 0.75 L = 6,750 L which rounds to the answer's 7,000 L. The arithmetic is self-consistent; the source is not one a verdict can rest on.

rows.claim: a bulk load in the same box carries roughly three times the volume
rows.note: Follows arithmetically from q2#2 on the same non-tier-1 source (24,000 L bulk vs ~6,750 L packaged = ~3.5x). Defensible as an order-of-magnitude point; not sourceable to a regulator, research institute or trade body.

rows.claim: commonly cited saving of the order of 30-40% in transport emissions per litre
rows.note: This is the riskiest number in the answer because it is precise, quotable and attributed to nobody. Searched Wine Australia (including the AWR-2201 LCA final report and the Emissions Reduction Roadmap), NZ Wine, OIV and ec.europa.eu. The Wine Australia LCA reports absolute kg CO2e/L by scenario rather than a bulk-versus-bottled percentage, and I could not extract the bulk-export module cleanly from the PDF. NZ Wine's LCA attributes 35% of emissions to packaging and 22% to shipping, which does not yield a 30-40% transport figure. The answer's own hedge 'a commonly cited saving' is honest and should be kept; do not harden it.

rows.claim: glass is the largest single component of a packaged wine's carbon footprint

source.ref: Cost, climate, consumers: influences on changes in wine packaging, Market Bulletin issue 297 (https://www.wineaustralia.com/news/market-bulletin/issue-297)
source.quote: Packaging is estimated to contributed 44 per cent of these emissions, with heavy glass bottles being the main contributor (34.4 per cent of total emissions).

rows.note: Corroborated by NZ Wine's food-miles LCA (packaging 35% of total emissions for a Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc, larger than shipping at 22%, 'namely due to embodied emissions of glass bottles'). Time-sensitive because lightweighting and higher cullet rates are actively moving the number down.

rows.claim: free SO2 is typically set higher at fill, of the order of 35-45 mg/L
rows.note: The principle is tier-1 supported — Bragato Research Institute: 'Free SO2 levels consistently decline during shipping as oxygen is absorbed and bound. The rate of this decline varies widely ... reinforcing the importance of conservative setpoints at dispatch' — but no source gives 35-45 mg/L. For context, AWRI's normal pre-bottling target for white table wine is 28-32 mg/L free and its survey of 3,167 Australian wines put the white median at 32 mg/L, so 35-45 is a plausible uplift but an unsourced one. AWRI's bulk-transport trial report is behind a levy-payer password.

rows.claim: container decks can exceed 40

source.publisher: OENO One (IVES open science) review of transport conditions; AWRI Technical Note TN09
source.quote: high variations in temperature (from -10°C to 67°C) in a shipping container; this can include a steady increase in temperature affecting wines shipped from winter temperatures to equator temperatures ... The most extreme shipping temperatures are experienced during the trans-shipment phase, since relay ports are often located close to the equator.

rows.note: Comfortably supported — the documented ceiling in shipping containers (67°C) is well above the 40°C the answer claims. Same review records that wines exposed to over 40°C 'even for a short time, showed visual and sensory changes'. Medium rather than high only because the studies cited are of bottled, not bulk, shipments.

rows.claim: several appellations, Rioja among them, require bottling within the region

source.ref: Estatutos / Reglamento DOCa Rioja, Artículo 32 (https://riojawine.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/Estatutos.pdf); corroborated by the Pliego de Condiciones 2021, b.10.5 'Embotellado en origen'
source.quote: El embotellado de vinos amparados por la denominación de origen calificada Rioja deberá ser realizado exclusivamente en las bodegas inscritas autorizadas por el Consejo Regulador, perdiendo el vino en otro caso el derecho al uso de la denominación.

rows.note: Registered bottling bodegas must be 'situadas en la zona de producción' (Art. 23), so the rule is a bottling-in-region rule in substance. Priorat's pliego carries an identical requirement, which would make a second example if one is wanted. Flagged time_sensitive because in-region bottling rules have repeatedly been litigated at EU level.

rows.claim: an internal bore of about 18.5 mm, and a natural cork of 24 mm diameter

source.publisher: CETIE (GME finish data sheets, citing EN 12726); AWRI
source.quote: CETIE: 'refer to the standard EN 12726 - PACKAGING - CORK MOUTH FINISH WITH A BORE DIAMETER OF 18,5 mm FOR CORKS AND TAMPER EVIDENT CAPSULES'. AWRI closure table lists lengths x diameters of 38 x 24, 44 x 24 and 49 x 24 mm.

rows.note: Both numbers check out: EN 12726 is the 18.5 mm cork mouth finish, and every closure size in AWRI's own extraction-force table is 24 mm diameter. Note the CETIE internal-diameter spec is a taper (18-19 mm at 3 mm depth, 19-21 mm at 45 mm depth), so '18.5 mm bore' is the nominal entry, not a constant.

rows.claim: up to 6 bar at 20

source.publisher: Comité Champagne (champagne.fr); Union des Maisons de Champagne
source.quote: Comité Champagne: 'The pressure inside a Champagne bottle is within the range of 5 to 6 bar.' UMC: 'the addition of the liqueur de tirage is precisely calculated to produce an increase in pressure of 6 kg/cm2 by the end of fermentation.'

rows.note: 'Up to 6 bar' is the right way to put it — the Comité Champagne gives 5-6 bar as the range and UMC gives 6 kg/cm2 as the tirage target. The '20°C' qualifier is also correct practice: OIV's method of analysis expresses sparkling-wine overpressure as Paph20, i.e. at 20°C.

rows.claim: reference dose of free SO2 at bottling of the order of 25-35 mg/L for a white

source.ref: Pre-bottling wine adjustments and specifications (https://www.awri.com.au/industry_support/winemaking_resources/storage-and-packaging/pre-packaging-preparation/pre-bottling-wine-adjustments-and-specifications/); corroborated by A snapshot of SO2 concentrations in Australian wines, Technical Review 236
source.quote: | **Free SO2** | mg/L | 28-32 [white table wine] | 28-32 [red table wine] | ... Free sulfur dioxide concentration should be considered based on wine pH

rows.note: AWRI's pre-bottling target is 28-32 mg/L free for white table wine, and its survey of 3,167 commercial Australian wines gives a white median of 32 mg/L (mean 31.0). The answer's 25-35 mg/L brackets that correctly. AWRI's caveat that the figure must be read against pH is the same point the answer makes elsewhere.

rows.claim: a 26 mm crown cap or a mushroom cork retained by a wirehood

source.quote: GME13.08 — Traditional Method Sparkling Wine Finishes: diameters 26 mm, 29 mm and 36 mm, for 'sparkling wine produced by the Traditional method', designed to take a crown cap and cork stopper combination.

rows.note: 26 mm is one of three standardised traditional-method crown finishes; 29 mm is the other common one (CETIE also publishes a dedicated 29 mm Spumante crown finish). Writing '26 mm' as if it were the only option is slightly narrow but is a real CETIE specification, so I would not correct it — a candidate could safely write 'a 26 or 29 mm crown cap'.

rows.claim: specified in the region of 20-40 daN

source.quote: Closure length (mm) 38 x 24: McMahon 230–400 N, CE.T.I.E 120–350 N; 44 x 24: McMahon 250–450 N, CE.T.I.E 120–400 N, synthetic 100–450 N; 49 x 24: McMahon 270–480 N.

rows.corrected_claim: cork extraction force is specified in the region of 12-45 daN depending on closure length and the standard applied
rows.note: 20-40 daN sits inside the real envelope but is narrower than any published spec. CETIE 2008 as reproduced by AWRI runs 12-40 daN; McMahon 1994 runs 23-48 daN; the Cork Quality Council's ISO 9727-5 specification for a 45 x 24 mm cork is 15-45 daN. The point the answer is making — that it is a purchased specification with a defined window — survives; the window is wider than stated.

rows.claim: a tin-Saran lined screwcap admits very little, of the order of 0.5 mg of oxygen a year

source.quote: The oxygen transmission rate (OTR) of Saran Tin liners is typically 0.00005-0.0005 cc O2/day, with the Saranex liner an order of magnitude higher at around 0.0001-0.001 cc O2/day.

rows.corrected_claim: a tin-Saran lined screwcap admits very little — roughly 0.02-0.2 cc, of the order of 0.03-0.3 mg, of oxygen a year — with a Saranex liner about an order of magnitude higher, nearer 0.5 mg a year
rows.note: The figure is misattributed to the wrong liner by roughly a factor of ten. AWRI's tin-Saran range of 0.00005-0.0005 cc O2/day works out at about 0.02-0.18 cc/year, i.e. roughly 0.03-0.26 mg O2/year. 0.5 mg/year is the Saranex number — the peer-reviewed closure trial in PMC9505717 specifies '30 × 60 mm ROPP Stelvin capsules with Saranex liners ... with an average OTR of 0.5 mg/year'. This matters in the answer's own argument, because the tin-Saran/Saranex gap is precisely why European producers choose Saranex to avoid reduction, a point the answer makes elsewhere.

rows.claim: natural cork admits roughly 0.5-2 mg a year

source.publisher: AWRI (qualitative); Oliveira et al. 2013, Amorim / University of Bordeaux (quantitative, reached via a Vinventions technical article)
source.quote: AWRI: 'Natural corks can show high levels of variability in their permeability, depending on the grade of cork used.' Oliveira et al.: a population of 600 corks tubed from only 2 planks varied 'from 0.5 to more than 4 mg of oxygen over 1 year'.

rows.corrected_claim: natural cork admits roughly 0.5 to more than 4 mg a year, and the variability between individual corks is itself the defining problem
rows.note: The lower bound is right and the upper bound truncates the tail that makes cork's case difficult. AWRI (tier-1) confirms high variability qualitatively but its fact sheet publishes the values only as a bar chart with no readable numbers; the 0.5-to->4 mg spread comes from an Amorim/University of Bordeaux study that I could only reach through a closure company's technical article, hence medium confidence. Correcting to '>4 mg' actually strengthens the answer's own argument for technical corks.

rows.claim: a co-extruded synthetic several times more again

source.publisher: AWRI; Nomacorc specifications as reported in a peer-reviewed closure trial (PMC9505717)
source.quote: AWRI: 'Synthetic closures typically possess values within the moderate to high OTR range, but there is significant variability among the products available.' Nomacorc Select 300 specification: '1.7 mg of O2 per year after the first year'.

rows.corrected_claim: a co-extruded synthetic sits in the moderate-to-high band, overlapping the upper end of natural cork rather than exceeding it several-fold
rows.note: 'Several times more again' overstates the gap. AWRI puts synthetics in the moderate-to-high range and natural cork in a wide, variable range that reaches the same territory; Nomacorc's own published steady-state figure of 1.7 mg O2/year sits inside natural cork's 0.5-to->4 mg envelope, not several times above it. The ordering of closure types is right; the multiplier is not supportable.

rows.claim: TCA is detectable at roughly 1.5-4 ng/L

source.ref: Wine flavours, faults and taints — Cork-type taints (https://www.awri.com.au/industry_support/winemaking_resources/sensory_assessment/recognition-of-wine-faults-and-taints/wine_faults/)
source.quote: One study determined the aroma threshold of TCA in a Pinot Noir wine as 1.4 ng/L ... the aroma threshold might be lower in dry, white wines or higher in full-bodied red wines. Prescott et al. (2005) reported that the consumer rejection threshold for TCA was 3.1 ng/L whilst the consumer detection threhsold was 2.1 ng/L ... the presence of TCA at a concentration as low as 1 ng/L suppressed the ratings for overall aroma intensity and of positive fruit-derived characters

rows.note: All three parts of this sentence are supported by one AWRI page: the detection band (1.4-3.1 ng/L across aroma, consumer detection and consumer rejection thresholds), the lower threshold in delicate whites, and the fruit suppression at 1 ng/L, below recognition as a fault. The strongest-sourced claim in the answer.

rows.claim: incidence has fallen from the several per cent widely reported in the 1990s to well under 1%
rows.note: The 1990s half is roughly supported — Virginia Tech Enology reports US cork-taint incidence 'to range from 0.5% to more than 2%', and AWRI's 2005 Advanced Wine Assessment Course found 16 of 470-odd bottles (3.4%) TCA-tainted. The 'well under 1% today' half I could not source anywhere tier-1: AWRI's recent annual reports discuss taint investigations as a share of helpdesk cases, not as a market incidence rate, and the sub-1% figures in circulation come from cork producers and their trade bodies. This is a number a candidate should attribute or soften, not assert.

rows.claim: a BVS 30 x 60 threaded finish

source.publisher: CETIE (GME30.15 BVP and BVS minimum through bore); peer-reviewed closure trial PMC9505717
source.quote: CETIE GME30.15: 'This data sheet specifies the values of the minimum through bore for BVP and BVS finishes.' PMC9505717 methods: 'Screw caps donated from Amcor were 30 × 60 mm ROPP Stelvin capsules'.

rows.note: BVS is a CETIE-standardised finish family and 30 x 60 is the format actually specified in the closure literature for wine screwcaps. Medium confidence because I confirmed the two halves separately (CETIE for BVS as a standard finish, the trial paper for the 30 x 60 dimension) rather than finding one document stating 'BVS 30 x 60'. The load-bearing point — that cork and screwcap need different glass, decided at bottle order — is not in doubt.

rows.claim: Grades run from coarse to fine, taking a wine of 50-100 NTU down to around 1-2 NTU

source.quote: Wines between 100 and 200 NTU may undergo macro-filtration steps from coarse metal screens to earth filtration, with a finer earth filtration conducted between 60 and 100 NTU. Once a wine is below 60 NTU, particulate matter is much smaller in size and pad filters (often in conjunction with earth filtration) or cross-flow filtration can be used

rows.corrected_claim: grades run from coarse to fine, taking a wine from 100-200 NTU down towards cellar-bright, with pads or cross-flow rather than earth doing the final cut to 1-3 NTU
rows.note: Earth filtration's working band per AWRI is 60-200 NTU, above the 50-100 NTU stated, and AWRI's own filter-grade table assigns 'final filtration for dry wines' at 1.0-3.0 NTU to sheets, not earth. Claiming earth filtration reaches 1-2 NTU overstates what a depth filter does and blurs the answer's own distinction between parts (a) and (b) of the question.

rows.claim: Dosage is of the order of 0.5-1.5 kg per 1,000 litres
rows.note: The closest tier-1 figure is Wine Australia's winery wastewater survey: 'DE use averaged 1.5 kg/tonne equivalent crush with a range of 0.0 to 8.2 kg/tonne', which is a whole-winery annual figure across all filtration steps and a different denominator from kg per 1,000 litres filtered. Same order of magnitude, but it does not verify the claim. No tier-1 source gives precoat/body-feed dosing rates per volume filtered.

rows.claim: respirable crystalline silica, a recognised carcinogen

source.publisher: IARC / WHO (Monographs Vol. 68 and Vol. 100C); corroborated by NIOSH
source.quote: Silica dust (crystalline, in the form of quartz or cristobalite) was previously classified by IARC as carcinogenic to humans (Group 1) in IARC Monographs Volume 100C in 2009 ... There is sufficient evidence that crystalline silica dust exposure causes lung cancer.

rows.note: Correct as written, and worth one clarifying detail if space allows: IARC's Group 1 classification is for crystalline silica (quartz/cristobalite); amorphous silica 'could not be classified'. Diatomite as mined is largely amorphous, but the flux-calcined grades used as filter aids contain cristobalite, which is exactly why the winery exposure is a crystalline-silica hazard. AWRI's practices survey independently records eliminating DE as a health-and-safety driver for cross-flow adoption.

rows.claim: coarse sheets clarifying to a few NTU, through fine sheets, to sterilising EK grades rated at about 0.4-0.6 microns

source.ref: Filtration – physical removal of microorganisms, 'What level of filtration do I need?' table (https://www.awri.com.au/industry_support/winemaking_resources/storage-and-packaging/pre-packaging-preparation/filtration-physical-removal-of-microorganisms/)
source.quote: Coarse filtration / First racking | 35-100 NTU | ... Final filtration for dry wines | 1.0-3.0 | 50H (0.8 µm), 60H (0.5 µm) ... Filtration for sweet wines, higher risk wines or final polish pre-membrane filtration | <1.0 | KS50 (0.5 µm), EK (0.4 µm) | Z7 (0.6 µm), Z8 (0.4 µm)

rows.note: The grade ladder and the EK rating both check out against AWRI's supplier-collated table: EK is rated 0.4 µm, with the neighbouring tightest grades at 0.4-0.6 µm, and sheet grades run from coarse (35-100 NTU duty) through polishing to that final band. The answer's '0.4-0.6 microns' is a fair reading of the table.

rows.claim: Sheets are dosed by area, of the order of one 40 x 40 cm sheet per 100-200 litres
rows.note: Searched AWRI, Wine Australia, Virginia Tech and OSU for sheet-filtration throughput per unit area. All describe plate-and-frame pad filtration and the 40 x 40 cm format is a real industry standard, but none publishes a litres-per-sheet dosing figure, so the 100-200 L per sheet cannot be verified either way. The surrounding assertions in the same sentence — single use, wine hold-up, blinding, and pre-flushing a new sheet to waste — are standard practice but likewise unsourced in the tier-1 corpus.

rows.claim: 0.65 microns as a prefilter, 0.45 microns for microbiological stability, which retains yeast and the great majority of spoilage bacteria, and 0.2 microns

source.quote: Surface filters are generally absolute filters with precisely defined maximum pore sizes and these include 0.65 µm and 0.45 µm or 'sterile' filtration. ... Most cross-flow membranes are only nominally rated at 0.2 µm which is theoretically tight enough for sterile filtration ... but as it is only a nominal rating, and can't be pressure tested for integrity before use, this means that wineries will still need to use a membrane filter if they want to achieve a sterile filtration.

rows.corrected_claim: the standard sizes are 0.65 microns as a prefilter and 0.45 microns for sterile filtration, which retains yeast and the great majority of spoilage bacteria; 0.2 microns is the nominal cross-flow rating and is used where absolute assurance is wanted
rows.note: 0.65 and 0.45 are exactly right. The imprecision is in demoting 0.45 µm to 'microbiological stability' and reserving 'sterility' for 0.2 µm: AWRI treats 0.45 µm as the sterile grade in wine, and introduces 0.2 µm as the nominal cross-flow membrane rating, which it explicitly says cannot be relied on for sterile filtration because it is nominal and not integrity-testable.

rows.claim: yeast cells are roughly 3-8 microns and most wine bacteria 0.5-2 microns

source.ref: Filtration – physical removal of microorganisms; Microbiological hazes and deposits; Classification of Particles (https://www.awri.com.au/industry_support/winemaking_resources/fining-stabilities/hazes_and_deposits/microbiological/)
source.quote: The human eye can detect large particulate matter >100 µm but not yeast and bacteria that are much smaller in size, around 0.5-5 µm in diameter. ... [lactic acid bacteria] Generally, their dimensions are approximately (0.5 – 1) x (1-2) µm

rows.corrected_claim: yeast and wine bacteria are roughly 0.5-5 microns across, with lactic acid bacteria around (0.5-1) x (1-2) microns
rows.note: The bacteria half is well supported — AWRI gives LAB as (0.5-1) x (1-2) µm, matching the claim. The yeast half is not: AWRI's stated range for yeast and bacteria together is 0.5-5 µm, so 8 µm exceeds it, and Virginia Tech's filtration notes put the average Saccharomyces diameter far lower still. I found no tier-1 source for 3-8 µm (the widely quoted 5-10 µm figure traces to Wikipedia, which is not admissible here). Safer to give the combined AWRI range.

rows.claim: integrity-tested by bubble point before and after every run

source.quote: Virginia Tech: 'membrane filters must be bubble tested, before, (possibly during) and after each day's run. If the membrane fails the integrity or bubble test, everything produced between that time and the previous test is suspect.' AWRI: 'The bubble point test can be conducted at the start of a bottling run before any wine is run through the filter and it shows the integrity of the filter being used and if any leaks are present.'

rows.note: Both the practice and the reason the answer gives for it — documented release of a bottling run — are supported. Virginia Tech states the pre- and post-run testing explicitly and draws exactly the traceability consequence the answer draws. AWRI also publishes the pass pressures (0.65 µm membrane 140 kPa, 0.45 µm 180 kPa, on water with air).

rows.claim: crossflow handles a feed at 100 NTU or higher

source.ref: Filtration – physical removal of microorganisms; AWRI Practices Survey Final Report (https://www.awri.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/AWRI_Practices_Survey_Final_Report.pdf)
source.quote: Once a wine is below 60 NTU ... pad filters (often in conjunction with earth filtration) or cross-flow filtration can be used ... These filters have gradually been replaced by centrifuge and cross-flow filtration alternatives, mainly to avoid the use of diatomaceous earth. ... Cross-flow filtration was by far the most commonly nominated new practice to have a positive impact in the last five years

rows.corrected_claim: crossflow handles a turbid feed and delivers wine bright enough to bottle, displacing earth and pads, though a membrane filter is still required for a sterile fill
rows.note: The substance — cross-flow replacing earth and pads, and delivering bottle-bright wine — is strongly supported by AWRI, including winemakers calling it the biggest quality advance in 25 years. Two refinements: AWRI places wine cross-flow in the sub-60 NTU band rather than at 100 NTU or higher (wide-bore cross-flow on lees is a different duty), and AWRI is explicit that a cross-flow membrane's 0.2 µm rating is nominal and not integrity-testable, so it does not remove the need for a membrane filter on a sterile line.

The 'roughly 0.1 pH per g/L' figure is a common practical rule of thumb used in real wine (which is buffered very differently from an isolated acid-in-water titration), but WSU's own tartaric-acid-in-water table shows a much shallower slope at the higher end of the range, so the fixed ratio should be presented as an approximation valid mainly in typical wine pH ranges rather than a universal constant.

rows.claim: removing about 0.75 g/L per gram added

rows.note: WSU's stoichiometric ratio inverts to ~1.49 g/L tartrate removed per 1 g/L KHCO3 added; AWRI's own empirical dosing table shows an average ~1.1 g/L TA decrease per 1 g/L KHCO3 addition. rows.corrected_claim: The EU ban on blending red wine into white to make rosé applies specifically to still wines without a protected designation of origin or geographical indication (non-PDO/PGI); PDO/PGI still rosés and any sparkling/semi-sparkling wine may use this blending method.
rows.note: The commonly stated 'total EU ban on blending for still rosé, exception only for sparkling' is an oversimplification of Article 8 of Reg 606/2009 (now 2019/934): the exclusion is for non-PDO/PGI wine specifically, not all still wine.

rows.claim: Argon is roughly 1.4 times the density of air and carbon dioxide roughly 1.5

source.ref: gases: carbon dioxide, argon, and nitrogen (Zoecklein)

rows.note: Calculation: for ideal gases at same T/P, density ratio = molar mass ratio. Argon/air = 39.95/28.97 (std air MW) = 1.38 ≈ 1.4. CO2/air = 44.01/28.97 = 1.52 ≈ 1.5. Matches the claim closely.

rows.claim: the same 25 mg/L free is protective at pH 3.2 and nearly inert at pH 3.7

source.quote: n/a — calculation

rows.note: Molecular fraction = 1/(1+10^(pH-pKa1)). At pH 3.2: fraction=0.039, so 25 mg/L free -> ~1.0 mg/L molecular (well above 0.5 mg/L protective threshold). At pH 3.7: fraction=0.0127, so 25 mg/L free -> ~0.32 mg/L molecular (below typical protective threshold). Confirms 'protective at 3.2, nearly inert at 3.7'.

rows.claim: DAP is roughly 21 per cent nitrogen by weight, so 10 g/hL raises YAN by about 21 mg N/L

rows.claim: the OIV ceiling for ammonium salts is 100 g/hL

source.quote: For nutritive salts, diammonium phosphate, or ammonium sulphate to a maximum dose of 0.3 g/l (expressed as the salt).

rows.corrected_claim: The 100 g/hL ceiling for ammonium salts (DAP) is an EU limit for nutrient additions during primary alcoholic fermentation, not an OIV limit. OIV's own code caps ammonium salts at 0.3 g/L (30 g/hL) — but that provision specifically governs nutrient additions to base wine for secondary (bottle) fermentation of sparkling wine, not primary fermentation of still wine.
rows.note: Confirmed via OIV Code Sheet 2024/2025 and independently via Enartis technical datasheet: 'Maximum legal dose in the EU: 100 g/hL in primary fermentation; 30 g/hL in second fermentation of sparkling wines' (Reg (EU) 2019/934). rows.note: Calculation: molecular fraction = 1/(1+10^(pH-1.81)). At pH 3.0, fraction = 0.0606, so 20 mg/L free gives ~1.21 mg/L molecular — about 2.4x the stated 0.5 mg/L target (only ~8-10 mg/L free would be needed for 0.5 mg/L molecular). By contrast pH 3.5 (fraction 0.020, 40 mg/L -> 0.8 mg/L) and pH 3.8 (fraction 0.0101, 80 mg/L -> 0.81 mg/L) both check out closely against a 0.8 mg/L target. This matches the known recurring error class of SO2/pH pairs implying the wrong molecular target — here specifically at the low-pH end of the table.
